records.content: On Wednesday President Donald Trump's latest nominee for surgeon general took steps to distance herself from the president's false statements on vaccinations by telling a Senate confirmation hearing that the shots are not the cause of autism. Trump announced the nomination of Nicole Saphier, a radiologist and Fox News personality, for the country's top public health position in April—she is the third nominee for the role since the second Trump administration began. Saphier replaced wellness influencer Casey Means, who had drawn fire from a bipartisan group of lawmakers for her stances toward vaccines and alternative medicine. During her testimony on Wednesday, Saphier tried to create distance between herself and positions taken by both Trump and U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert Kennedy, Jr. Saphier told lawmakers that she does not know what causes autism, and she has "not seen reputable evidence that would suggest that vaccines cause autism." When questioned about Trump's recent claim that the mumps, measles and rubella vaccine may be "lethal," Saphier responded by describing the shot as "our greatest tool for combating measles." Almost 3,300 cases of measles have been confirmed in the U.S. this year as of September 11, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention—an increase of more than 1,000 compared with the cases reported for all of 2025. Four deaths have been linked to the current outbreak, the most since 1992. When asked for comment, White House spokesperson Kush Desai called Saphier an "accomplished physician who has practiced radiology at Memorial Sloan Kettering and has been an outspoken voice on breast cancer prevention, intrusive COVID-19 mandates, the politicization of science and the federal government's role in America's chronic disease epidemic. She has been a powerful asset for President Trump and works tirelessly to deliver on every facet of his MAHA agenda." Saphier also expressed support for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth—a long-standing CDC recommendation that Kennedy and other top Trump health officials have taken steps to eliminate. "The hepatitis B vaccines are one of the most tangible ways we have to prevent cancer, and that is something that I absolutely am always excited about because it is so hard to prevent cancer in so many patients," she said, referring to the hepatitis B vaccine's protective effect against hepatitis-related liver cancers. Saphier's nomination has been criticized by several public health advocacy groups. In a statement issued on Wednesday, Defend Public Health coordinating committee member Julie Scofield said Saphier is "exactly the wrong person to be Surgeon General." "She has no background in public health, and it shows," Scofield said. "Saphier has argued that 'personal responsibility' is key to improving Americans' overall health—an idea that contradicts the basic tenets of public health, which recognize that our health is affected by many factors an individual simply can't control." At today's hearing, Saphier stressed the importance of Americans personally taking steps to reduce their chances of becoming ill and added that providing more information to the public on prevention will be a priority if she's confirmed. "There are small, tangible lifestyle modifications that people can do," Saphier said. "That doesn't mean that you have to become a nutrition expert or a someone who's at the gym every single day. But there are small modifications that people can do that will drastically reduce their risk of illness." Wednesday's confirmation hearing also featured testimony from two other nominees. The course led by WHO/Europe consultant, Professor Alexander Nersesov, aims to enhance the capacity of Turkmen medical professionals in their effort to combat viral hepatitis B. The skill-building session was conducted at the Infectious disease treatment-prevention center in videoconference mode. The participants of the event were doctors specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of viral hepatitis from the Infectious disease treatment-prevention center of the Directorate of Infectious Diseases Centers, primary health care providers, infectious diseases specialists from the institutions at the district level, and representatives from the department of infectious diseases at the State Medical University named after Myrat Karryev. The training covered essential information on hepatitis B, its diagnosis, classification, and treatment, with specific guidance for chronic cases, pregnancy, and special patient groups, as well as hepatitis D. This training is designed to equip medical professionals with the updated knowledge and best practices in viral hepatitis B diagnosis and treatment, aligning with both WHO guidelines and national protocols. By enhancing the skills of healthcare providers, this initiative will contribute to improved patient outcomes and strengthen Turkmenistan's efforts to control and manage viral hepatitis. Here’s What You Should Know By Erica Selorm Kabe Health & Fitness THU, 17 SEP 2026 Have you ever heard someone say, “I’m blood group O, so I hardly get sick,” or wondered whether your blood group could protect you from certain diseases? Most of us know our blood groups mainly because of blood transfusion, pregnancy or blood donation. We are usually identified as blood group A, B, AB or O and as either Rh positive or Rh negative. But could these differences actually affect our chances of contracting infections such as HIV or Hepatitis B? It is an interesting question, and one that scientists have investigated. But there is an important message everyone should understand: your blood group should never be considered protection against HIV or Hepatitis B. What Does Your Blood Group Really Mean? Our ABO blood groups are determined by certain substances, known as antigens, found on the surface of red blood cells. People with blood group A have A antigens, those with group B have B antigens, people with AB have both, while people with blood group O have neither A nor B antigens. Scientists have studied these biological differences to determine whether they are associated with susceptibility to various diseases and infections. Some studies have reported associations between particular blood groups and certain diseases. However, finding an association does not mean that a particular blood group directly causes a disease or guarantees protection from it. What About HIV and Hepatitis B? HIV attacks the body's immune system. It can be transmitted through certain body fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk. It can also be transmitted from mother to child. HIV is not spread through ordinary contact such as hugging, shaking hands or sharing food. Hepatitis B is caused by the Hepatitis B virus (HBV), which attacks the liver. The infection can become chronic and, over time, may lead to serious complications such as liver cirrhosis and liver cancer. HBV can be transmitted through infected blood and other body fluids, during sex, through contaminated sharp instruments and from an infected mother to her baby. Because these infections interact with the human body in complex ways, researchers have investigated whether characteristics such as ABO and Rh blood groups are associated with differences in infection patterns. However, research findings have varied among different populations. Therefore, your blood group alone cannot reliably tell whether you will or will not contract HIV or Hepatitis B. Why This Matters in Ghana HIV remains an important public health issue in Ghana. According to Ghana's 2025 National HIV Estimates and Projections, more than 337,000 people were estimated to be living with HIV in the country. This makes accurate public information about HIV prevention particularly important. Hepatitis B is also a major health concern because a person can be infected without initially showing obvious symptoms. Chronic infection can eventually cause severe liver disease. These realities make prevention, testing and reliable health information far more useful than assumptions based on one's blood group. Don't Let Your Blood Group Give You False Confidence Whether you are blood group O, A, B or AB, positive or negative, you should not consider yourself naturally protected from HIV or Hepatitis B. For HIV, prevention includes knowing your status, practising safer sex, avoiding the sharing of contaminated needles and sharp objects, and using recommended preventive services such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) when appropriate. People living with HIV who receive effective antiretroviral treatment can live long and healthy lives. Effective treatment can also reduce the amount of HIV in the blood to an undetectable level, at which point HIV is not sexually transmitted. For Hepatitis B, there is another powerful preventive tool: vaccination. The World Health Organization identifies Hepatitis B vaccination as an effective way of preventing the infection. Testing is equally important. You cannot determine someone's HIV or Hepatitis B status simply by looking at them—or by knowing their blood group. Know Your Status, Not Just Your Blood Group There is nothing wrong with knowing whether you are A+, B+, AB-, O+ or any other blood type. That information is medically useful. But knowing your blood group should not replace knowing your HIV or Hepatitis B status. Scientific research into blood groups and infectious diseases helps us better understand how biological differences between individuals may relate to patterns of disease. However, for the general public, the practical message is simple: No blood group should be treated as a shield against HIV or Hepatitis B. Get tested when appropriate. Practise recommended preventive measures. Find out whether you have been adequately vaccinated against Hepatitis B and seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional where necessary. Your blood group may tell us something interesting about your biology, but when it comes to HIV and Hepatitis B, prevention, vaccination where available, testing and appropriate medical care remain far more important than the letter attached to your blood type. Research may continue to uncover interesting links between blood groups and different diseases, but one message remains clear: do not depend on your blood group to protect you. Depend on knowledge, prevention and timely healthcare. Know your blood group but more importantly, know your status and protect your health. Robert G. Gish, MD A newer generation of capsid assembly modulators may finally move the needle on surface antigen, something earlier compounds in this class could not achieve. This episode explores that shift. Advertisement Episodes in this series Previous slideNext slide EP. 1 Understanding the Immune Pathophysiology Driving Chronic Hepatitis B EP. 2 Hepatitis B Epidemiology: Closing the Screening and Diagnosis Gap EP. 3 Monitoring Disease Progression and Liver Cancer Risk in Hepatitis B EP. 4 Quantitative HBsAg Testing and the Path to Finite-Duration Therapy EP. 5 Unmet Needs and Long-Term Antiviral Safety in Hepatitis B Care EP. 6 Why Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Cures Are Fundamentally Different EP. 7 The Next Frontier in Hepatitis B Functional and Virologic Cure EP. 8 Rethinking Standard of Care and the Promise of Functional Cure EP. 9 How Bepirovirsen Targets the Hepatitis B Viral Lifecycle EP. 10 Inside the Be-Well Trials: Design, Population, and Patient Selection EP. 11 Weighing Efficacy and Safety Data for an Emerging Hepatitis B Therapy Now Playing EP. 12 Capsid Assembly Modulators and the Case for Combination Therapy In "Capsid Assembly Modulators and the Case for Combination Therapy," the panel turns to a less mature but promising class of therapy targeting viral capsid assembly. Dr. Chung shifts to other, less mature classes of therapy, starting with pevifoscovir, also known as ALG-001075, describing in vitro data suggesting it works through several mechanisms, including direct antiviral activity blocking HBV DNA production, blocking cccDNA establishment, and potentially inhibiting e-antigen secretion. He asks Dr. Gish to explain its mechanism, how it compares with current standard of care, and how to interpret recent monotherapy findings showing sustained antigen reductions after 24 weeks of entecavir in a small cohort of e-antigen-positive patients. Dr. Gish says he has been excited about capsid assembly modulators, sometimes called CAMs or CpAMs, since this class emerged, describing pevifoscovir as a true second- or third-generation compound. He explains that this class includes drugs producing empty capsids and others producing aberrant capsids, both altering viral secretion and reducing infection of other cells, which decreases total viral replication and release. He notes that pevifoscovir's surface antigen data appear to be the first meaningful signal for this drug class, since an earlier compound in the same category did not affect surface antigen and saw resistance and relapse after stopping therapy. He believes pevifoscovir could compete directly against nucleoside analogs, which rarely reduce surface antigen meaningfully, achieving only about 5% at five years with entecavir or tenofovir-based regimens. He also describes cccDNA as constantly recycled and re-established in the nucleus, but notes that natural endonuclease activity degrades it over time, so interrupting that replenishment cycle may allow natural clearance. He credits earlier work suggesting this concept, though he believes pevifoscovir has stronger supporting data. Looking ahead, he expects combination regimens of two to four compounds, rather than any single agent, to ultimately deliver surface antigen clearance and functional cure. In "Can Innate Immune Agonists Help Deliver Hepatitis B Cure?," the panel will unpack a therapy working through an entirely different, innate immune pathway. 慢乙肝是免疫介导性疾病,免疫重建是实现治愈的关键 慢乙肝本质上是免疫介导性疾病, HBV破坏机体的先天免疫和适应性免疫,驱动感染慢性化,机体无法清除病毒,导致感染持续存在[1,2]。肝内cccDNA和整合HBV DNA及其持续产生的HBsAg等病毒抗原,导致先天免疫和适应性免疫受损。其中,HBV特异性CD8+ T细胞是清除HBV病毒的核心效应细胞[3],但因长期抗原暴露及肝脏耐受性微环境等因素发生功能障碍与耗竭[4],致使机体丧失清除HBV及受感染肝细胞的能力。持续HBV病毒复制与肝脏炎症损伤,进一步促进乙肝疾病进展。因此,重建对HBV的免疫应答是实现乙肝治愈的关键。 HBV及其产生的病毒抗原导致先天免疫和适应性免疫受损[2] 02 联合治疗是未来的必然趋势,免疫是持久临床治愈的核心 实现乙肝治愈的策略有两种途径,一是在不杀死受感染肝细胞的情况下治愈乙肝,如通过基因编辑、表观遗传修饰等清除或永久沉默cccDNA,目前还无法实现;二是诱导免疫调节,安全清除HBV感染的肝细胞。“降低病毒负荷”+“强效免疫调节”是未来实现临床治愈的必然趋势。 靶向HBV生命周期的药物,如ASO/siRNA虽然能够快速降低HBsAg,但几乎无免疫调节作用,停药后复发率高,难以实现持久的临床治愈。例如备受瞩目的ASO药物Bepirovirsen(GSK836)于2026年8月在日本正式获批上市,目前在中国上市时间仍然未知。本次日本获批依据两项全球多中心III期临床试验,B-Well 1和B-Well 2研究表明对于核苷经治100 ≤ HBsAg < 3000 IU/mL的慢乙肝患者,经Bepirovirsen联合NA治疗的临床治愈率分别为20%和19%[5]。需要客观看待的是,该药物适用人群存在明确限制,仍有大部分患者无法从中获益,而且HBsAg清除后的复阳率超过60%,其远期疗效与长期安全性仍有待真实世界数据进一步验证。 针对免疫调节的新型药物,比如治疗性疫苗、TLR7/8/9激动剂、单克隆抗体、PD-1/PD-L1抑制剂等目前疗效均有限。因此,只有强效的免疫调节,能有效激活先天免疫和适应性免疫,才是实现持久临床治愈的核心。 降低病毒负荷和宿主免疫重建的治疗策略[6] 03 PegIFNα具有强效免疫调节作用,是实现慢乙肝临床治愈的基石药物 聚乙二醇干扰素α(PegIFNα)是目前免疫调节作用最强效的乙肝药物,同时具有直接抗病毒和免疫调节的双重作用[7],因此是实现慢乙肝临床治愈的基石药物。在直接抗病毒方面,PegIFNα可通过直接抗病毒作用抑制HBV生命周期的全过程,降低HBV DNA、HBeAg、HBsAg、HBV RNA,更重要的是可降低cccDNA,从源头抑制病毒。在免疫调节方面,PegIFNα通过免疫重建,实现免疫清除,建立长期的免疫记忆,实现持久的临床治愈。 3.1 免疫重建——主动打破免疫耐受,激活机体免疫 PegIFNα协同激活先天与适应性免疫,实现对慢乙肝的免疫重建[8]。PegIFNα广泛调控多种免疫细胞:增强树突状细胞(DC)的抗原提呈能力,放大NK细胞应答、增强其细胞毒活性;通过诱导巨噬细胞等肝非实质细胞产生外泌体,强化整体抗病毒效应;提高浆细胞比例,促进抗病毒中和抗体生成;促进CD8+、CD4+ T淋巴细胞活化,进而提升细胞因子分泌水平与细胞毒性T淋巴细胞(CTL)应答效能。 PegIFNα实现对慢乙肝的免疫重建[8] 3.2 免疫清除——降低病毒负荷,清除受感染肝细胞 PegIFNα可通过非溶细胞性和溶细胞性两种途径清除HBV感染。非溶细胞性清除主要通过细胞因子可在不杀伤肝细胞的条件下抑制乃至清除HBV。溶细胞性清除是消除HBV最直接的方式,主要依赖细胞毒性T淋巴细胞的作用,并有NK和自然杀伤 T 细胞(NKT)等协同参与,杀伤受感染肝细胞,实现免疫清除。 清除HBV感染的主要途径[9] 3.3 免疫记忆——建立长期免疫,实现持久临床治愈 PegIFNα治疗可促进慢乙肝患者记忆T细胞的恢复,应答者在体外再次遇到病毒抗原时表现出快速而强烈的记忆应答[10]。同时,PegIFNα治疗可有效恢复HBsAg特异性B细胞的活化状态与IgG+ 经典记忆B细胞分化,并促进HBsAb产生[11],有利于临床治愈持久性。 3.4 临床治愈后多重获益 正是PegIFNα这种强效且持久的免疫调节机制,使得基于PegIFNα的治疗方案能使慢乙肝患者治疗获益最大化。一项III期临床治愈RCT研究显示,NAs经治患者基于PegIFNα-2b联合TDF治疗的临床治愈率达31.4%[12],临床治愈患者延长随访104周时的维持率高达约90%[13]。此外,临床治愈后具有多重获益,其肝脏内免疫环境明显改善[14],肝内cccDNA和整合HBV DNA显著降低[15,16],肝癌发生风险降至最低[17,18]。 04 讨 论 综合来看,未来联合治疗是实现乙肝临床治愈的必然趋势,“降低病毒负荷+强效免疫调节”是关键策略,免疫是持久临床治愈的核心。GSK836等新型药物的III期数据已经表明,缺乏强效持久免疫调节的药物,即使能在短期内降低HBsAg,停药复阳率高的问题仍无法解决。免疫调节剂如PD-1/PD-L1抑制剂、TLR激动剂等疗效十分有限。PegIFNα凭借其不可替代的免疫调节机制——免疫重建、免疫清除、免疫记忆,是目前最强效的免疫调节药物,因此是联合治疗的基石药物,未来不同药物如何联合、联合时机、具体疗程仍需要进一步探索。 先前GSK836序贯PegIFNα治疗的II期B-Together研究显示,更早序贯PegIFNα,复发率越低[19]。这提示更早开始PegIFNα治疗,可在一定量抗原暴露窗口下提升有效的免疫识别,重建对HBV的适应性免疫应答,才能实现对受感染肝细胞的持续清除及免疫控制,最终达到持久的临床治愈。因此,PegIFNα与ASO/siRNA的联合治疗策略应前置PegIFNα,让免疫重建先行,为后续的联合增效夯实基础。以PegIFNα巩固可建立长期的免疫记忆。 此外,PegIFNα与CAM、治疗性疫苗等的联合也值得进一步探索。未来需在机制协同的基础上,通过临床试验进一步明确联合时机、疗程长短与不同人群分层管理,真正将“降低病毒负荷+强效免疫调节”的核心策略转化为可落地的持久治愈方案。 参考文献: [1] Yuen MF, Chen DS, Dusheiko GM, et al. Now a team at the Institute of Microbiology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, working with colleagues at Capital Medical University, has uncovered a molecular gatekeeper behind this decline. Reporting in Nature Immunology, Wei Xu and colleagues show that ANKRD11, a chromatin-associated protein, acts as a brake on CD8+ T cell effector differentiation, and that removing this brake dramatically enhances antiviral and antitumor immunity in mouse models. The study began with a practical problem: researchers have lacked good tools to study the behavior of hepatitis B virus-specific T cells in a physiologically relevant setting. The team used a humanized mouse model carrying the human HLA-A11 molecule to identify a T cell receptor that recognizes HBc141-151, an epitope from the hepatitis B core antigen that is clinically relevant in human patients. This receptor, which the authors call HB-I, allowed them to generate transgenic mice whose entire CD8+ T cell population is specific for a single, human-relevant HBV epitope, providing a tractable platform for dissecting why these cells fail during chronic infection. With that platform in hand, the researchers turned to an unbiased discovery strategy. Using a whole-genome CRISPR-Cas9 knockout library delivered into HBV-specific T cells, followed by screening under chronic antigen stimulation, they asked which genes, when deleted, would help T cells resist the dysfunctional state that normally develops. The screen converged on Ankrd11, a gene previously known as a chromatin regulator implicated in neural development and in Kabuki-like syndromes, but never before linked to T cell exhaustion. Loss of Ankrd11 consistently produced T cells that proliferated more vigorously and retained stronger effector characteristics. Discover more Cancer genes Medical Literature & Resources Genetic Disorders Biological Sciences The mechanistic picture that emerges from the paper is epigenetic. ANKRD11 appears to restrain the accessibility and acetylation of key effector genes. Using ATAC-seq, bulk RNA-seq and CUT&Tag profiling of the histone mark H3K27ac, the team showed that Ankrd11-deficient CD8+ T cells display increased chromatin openness and enhancer acetylation at loci encoding AP-1 family transcription factors, notably Fos and Fosb. Elevated AP-1 activity, in turn, drives a program of effector differentiation: the cells produce more granzyme B and interferon-gamma, resist the immunosuppressive conditions that normally silence them, and maintain function even when interleukin-2, a survival factor, is limiting. Functionally, the consequences of losing this brake were striking. In mice carrying a replicating HBV plasmid or infected with recombinant HBV vectors, Ankrd11-deficient HBV-specific T cells expanded more robustly, infiltrated the liver more effectively, and drastically reduced serum levels of hepatitis B surface antigen, viral DNA and markers of liver damage. Parallel experiments using a second chronic infection model, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus clone 13, confirmed the generality of the effect: adoptively transferred Ankrd11-deficient virus-specific P14 T cells showed enhanced granzyme expression, proliferation and viral control in the spleen and blood. Perhaps the most conceptually interesting finding concerns the differentiation paths that exhausted T cells normally follow. In chronic infection and cancer, antigen-specific CD8+ T cells split into progenitor exhausted T cells, which express the transcription factor TCF-1 and serve as a self-renewing reservoir, and terminally exhausted T cells, which lose TCF-1 and are irreversibly dysfunctional. The authors found that Ankrd11 deficiency accelerates the conversion of progenitor exhausted cells into effector-like exhausted cells, but importantly, the resulting cells are cytotoxic and functional rather than inert. This suggests ANKRD11 does not simply maintain progenitor pools but actively gates how far exhausted cells differentiate toward effector competence. The study also revealed a distinct route of reprogramming specific to chronic hepatitis B. A large fraction of HBV-specific CD8+ T cells in tolerant mice carries a PD-1-negative, TOX-negative phenotype that has resisted conventional checkpoint-based rescue strategies. When ANKRD11-mediated repression was relieved, these tolerant cells differentiated into PD-1-positive, KLRG1-positive effector cells armed with high granzyme levels, providing an explanation for the improved viral clearance. In other words, ANKRD11 deficiency unlocks an otherwise dormant pool of virus-specific cells that immune checkpoint blockade alone cannot reach. Discover more Genetics Infectious Diseases gene Colleges & Universities Postdoc Position Listings The antitumor implications were tested directly in cancer models. Ankrd11-deficient CD8+ T cells promoted rejection of implanted tumors, enhanced intratumoral T cell activity, and acted synergistically with immune checkpoint blockade, potentiating the effect of PD-1 pathway inhibition. Given that the exhaustion of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes is a central cause of immunotherapy failure, a single gene whose deletion reprograms effector differentiation under immunosuppressive conditions is an attractive candidate for therapeutic engineering, for example in chimeric antigen receptor or T cell receptor-engineered cell products. A provisional patent application has been filed based on the findings, underscoring the translational interest. Caveats remain before ANKRD11 targeting reaches the clinic. ANKRD11 is a broad chromatin regulator with established roles in neural and cardiac development, so systemic inhibition is unlikely to be safe; the therapeutic window will probably lie in ex vivo engineering of T cells or in carefully targeted delivery. It will also be important to determine whether accelerated terminal differentiation comes at the cost of long-term memory formation. Nevertheless, the study delivers a clear conceptual advance: T cell dysfunction in chronic infection and cancer is not merely the product of inhibitory receptor signaling, but is epigenetically authored, and specific chromatin factors such as ANKRD11 can be removed to rewrite that script. For the hundreds of millions of people living with chronic hepatitis B, and for cancer patients whose T cells have gone quiet, that insight opens a new direction for immunotherapy design. The concept of T cell exhaustion has shaped immunology for two decades. Since the landmark demonstration that chronically stimulated CD8+ T cells can regain function when inhibitory pathways are interrupted, researchers have catalogued a molecular signature of the dysfunctional state, and later work established the transcription factor TOX as a master architect of the exhaustion program, acting at both transcriptional and epigenetic levels. What has remained less clear is whether exhaustion is a fixed fate or a tunable state whose chromatin underpinnings can be deliberately rewritten. The new study adds weight to the second view by identifying a specific chromatin-associated protein whose removal shifts the balance of differentiation toward cytotoxic competence. The methodological route to this finding is worth noting. Genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screens have become a powerful way to uncover genes that constrain or enable T cell behavior, and previous efforts using this approach identified regulators such as REGNASE-1 and Roquin as suppressors of effector expansion and antitumor immunity. The present screen extends this logic into the setting of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, a context in which suppressive cues differ from those in tumors and in which conventional checkpoint blockade has shown only modest clinical benefit. That an unbiased screen converged on a gene with no prior immunological pedigree illustrates how phenotype-first discovery can bypass assumptions rooted in known pathways. ANKRD11 itself carries an interesting dual history. It was first characterized as a chromatin regulator essential for neural development, and subsequent work showed it controls cardiac neural crest-mediated remodeling of the outflow tract. Its association with a Kabuki-like syndrome in humans reflects the pleiotropic consequences of disturbing a factor that operates broadly across tissues. This background both explains why the protein had escaped attention in immunology and reinforces the caution that any therapeutic interference must be confined to engineered cells rather than delivered systemically. The AP-1 connection provides a mechanistic bridge to earlier T cell biology. AP-1 family transcription factors, built from Fos and Jun proteins, have long been recognized as immediate-early responders to T cell receptor signaling, and their activity is known to cooperate with other factors to specify effector genes. By showing that ANKRD11 restrains chromatin accessibility and H3K27 acetylation at AP-1 loci, the study suggests a route by which a chromatin regulator can gate a transcriptional program that is otherwise primed and waiting in naive and exhausted cells alike. The authors have deposited the datasets underlying these conclusions in public repositories: bulk RNA-seq data under accession GSE299520, ATAC-seq data under GSE299519, and CUT&Tag data under GSE299521, with source data provided alongside the paper. No original code was generated. This transparency should allow groups working on T cell engineering to interrogate the chromatin changes directly and to test whether similar ANKRD11-sensitive programs operate in human tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, a necessary step before the findings can inform next-generation cell therapy design. Meanwhile, information from the World Cancer Research Fund indicates that in 2022, Thailand had the fourth highest liver cancer mortality rate in the world. The major issue is that most patients are usually diagnosed at the late stage and cannot be completely cured. Therefore, liver cancer screening is extremely important, because if detected at an early stage, it can increase the chances of complete treatment or at least improve the patient’s quality of life and longevity. Key Takeaways Liver cancer is a common type of cancer and is the leading cause of death among Thai people. Risk factors that may cause liver cancer include hepatitis B and C virus infection, cirrhosis, fatty liver disease, alcohol consumption, smoking, or exposure to Aflatoxin. Early-stage liver cancer usually does not show symptoms, causing many patients to be diagnosed at an advanced stage, which makes treatment more difficult. Annual health check-ups and hepatitis B vaccination help reduce the risk of liver cancer. Early detection increases the chances of complete treatment and maintaining quality of life. Understanding ‘Liver Cancer’: The Silent Danger Number One That Thai People Should Be Careful Of Liver cancer, or Hepatocellular Carcinoma, is cancer that occurs in the liver, caused by liver cells that undergo mutations and divide continuously without control. These cells multiply to form malignant tumors in the liver and can spread to other organs in the body. In Thailand, liver cancer is one of the most common cancers and is a leading cause of death, particularly in men, who are much more likely to develop the disease than women. The danger of the disease usually lies in late detection, so when diagnosed, many patients are already in the advanced stage, which is difficult to cure. What Causes Liver Cancer? Normal cells in the body have a process to control cell growth. However, mutated cells lose this control and divide abnormally, forming malignant tumors that can invade or spread to other organs. Several factors can lead to liver cancer, as follows: Chronic hepatitis B and C virus infection, a major cause commonly found in Thailand. Cirrhosis from various causes, such as regular alcohol consumption or liver damage from autoimmune disorders. Fatty liver disease, especially in cases of obesity, diabetes, or high blood lipid levels. Smoking. Exposure to certain toxins, such as Aflatoxin in fungi. Genetics. Male sex. Symptoms of Liver Cancer: Watch Early Before It’s Too Late Liver cancer is dangerous because, in the early stage, patients often show no abnormal symptoms or do not notice them, especially those who already have liver disease. As the disease progresses, liver cancer patients may experience the following symptoms: Fluid in the abdomen or abdominal enlargement Fullness, abdominal pain, or bloating Palpable mass in the abdomen Dark urine Weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue, weakness Diarrhea or black stools Numbness or cramps in hands and feet Low blood sugar, sweating, fainting Skin or muscle inflammation Jaundice, itching Bone pain Internal bleeding, anemia Who is at Risk for Liver Cancer? Those at risk for liver cancer include: Individuals with relatives who have liver disease or family history of liver cancer Individuals with chronic hepatitis B or C Individuals with iron overload in the liver (Hemochromatosis) Individuals with genetic disorders such as Tyrosinemia Individuals with cirrhosis Individuals exposed to Aflatoxin from fungi, commonly found in stored crushed peanuts or old chili powder Individuals with liver inflammation due to fatty liver disease Diagnosis of Liver Cancer Whether showing abnormal symptoms or at risk for liver cancer, screening and diagnosis should be performed using the following methods: Medical history and physical examination by a physician Blood tests to assess liver function, measure liver cancer marker Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP), and detect hepatitis viruses Radiological examinations such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI Biopsy for cancer examination Treatment Options for Liver Cancer Treatment depends on the severity or stage of the disease and the patient’s overall condition. Doctors often use multiple methods together to control the spread of cancer cells, as follows: Hepatic Resection Partial liver resection is the most effective liver cancer treatment, offering higher chances of complete cure compared to other methods. It is suitable for early-stage patients with small tumors that have not spread, normal liver function, and overall good health. Thermal Ablation Thermal ablation destroys liver cancer cells using heat. It is suitable for early-stage patients with small tumors. The treatment results are nearly comparable to liver surgery, but recurrence risk is slightly higher. It is an option for patients with impaired liver function or poor overall health unsuitable for surgery. Liver Transplantation Liver transplantation involves removing the diseased liver and replacing it with a new one. Limitations include finding a matching donor liver, risk of organ rejection, and lifelong immunosuppressive drugs affecting long-term immunity. It is used for patients with non-metastatic liver cancer and concurrent cirrhosis. Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE) TACE delivers chemotherapy directly to the tumor or its supplying blood vessel while blocking blood flow, causing the tumor to die. It is chosen when liver cancer has begun to spread or surgery is not feasible due to tumor location near large vessels, cirrhosis, or high surgical risk. Systemic Chemotherapy Systemic chemotherapy, including targeted therapy or immunotherapy, specifically attacks cancer cells to destroy or inhibit their division. It is available in injectable and oral forms. Radiotherapy Radiotherapy destroys liver cancer cells using focused radiation, without affecting surrounding organs or causing side effects. Palliative Care Palliative care does not aim to cure the disease but alleviates pain from liver cancer, improving the patient’s quality of life. Can Liver Cancer Be Prevented? Liver cancer arises from multiple factors but can be prevented by maintaining health and avoiding risk behaviors: Avoid alcohol and smoking Be cautious with foods potentially contaminated with Aflatoxin, such as peanuts, dried chili, or moldy onions Control diet, reduce high-fat and high-starch foods Exercise regularly Avoid hepatitis virus infection, do not share personal items, and receive hepatitis vaccination Undergo liver cancer screening, especially for high-risk groups such as those with cirrhosis, hepatitis virus infection, or family history of liver cancer Liver Cancer: Early Awareness Increases Chances of Cure Liver cancer is common and has a high mortality rate because most cases are detected at an advanced stage. However, good hygiene, regular annual health check-ups, and hepatitis B vaccination can reduce risk. Early detection and timely treatment provide a chance for complete cure and the restoration of a good quality of life. records.content: British pharmaceutical company GSK is turning to patient data gathered from the 88 million residents of the Greater Bay Area’s 11 cities to speed up drug development in vaccines and cancer care, as officials push for closer cross-border medical cooperation . GSK Hong Kong and Macau general manager Nicholas Teo said patient data was very important because it could form “supplementary evidence” to support regulatory filings and potential label expansions, and also help to “discover benefits other than the medication itself”. Vaccines were one example, Teo said last week. While their effectiveness against target diseases such as flu, shingles and respiratory syncytial virus was well established, he said researchers were increasingly studying potential benefits relating to cardiovascular health and neurological outcomes, which might help generate additional evidence and insights for future healthcare decision-making. Teo said GSK’s expertise lay in vaccination and disease prevention, citing shingles and respiratory syncytial virus as key areas, with the viral liver infection hepatitis B another area of focus. He added that GSK also had a growing oncology and haematology portfolio. View in App READ FULL ARTICLE The bay area is a government scheme aimed at integrating Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in mainland China’s Guangdong province into a single economic and business hub. Their combined gross domestic product last year was more than US$2.23 trillion, according to official data. GSK signed a memorandum of understanding in September last year with the University of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute on a study to examine the long-term health effects of the shingles vaccine. Teo said GSK would provide financial sponsorship for the HKU-led study and was also investing in shared data infrastructure. The company could access patient data through the partnership, such as data coming from hospitals and government agencies, but pharmaceutical companies did not have direct access to it on their own, he added. The institute, based in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and set up by the Hong Kong government, enables the free exchange of researchers and data between the two cities. Better decisions are made after we have better data Nicholas Teo, GSK Hong Kong and Macau He said real-world data was patient data gathered during routine clinical practice at hospitals and clinics. HKU pharmacy professor Ian Wong said at the conference that cross-border research required “infrastructure that’s safe enough” as the first pillar, alongside government regulation, ethics and public education, before real-world data could be used effectively. Raphael Yeung, a senior pharmacist at Hong Kong’s Drug Office, said the city had multiple regulatory safeguards in place, including the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Teo said the value of data ultimately came down to better outcomes and better policy. “Better decisions are made after we have better data,” he said. “If we have data that tells you a certain medication or vaccine benefits a particular population, the government can take a decision on whether to make it available, subsidise it, or improve access.” Teo added that GSK wanted to help prove that the cross-border data pipeline could work at scale. “We hope to be part of potential pilot studies or collaborations that will prove this data flow is safe, secure and high quality between Hong Kong and mainland China,” he said

records.content_title: Plasma Cystatin C as a Marker of Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure and 28-Day Mortality in Patients With Acutely Decompensated Liver Cirrhosis: A Prospective Observational Study
records.content: Abstract Background: Acute decompensation of cirrhosis carries a 28-day mortality of 1.9%, rising to nearly 30% with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), in which renal failure is the most frequent and most ominous organ failure. Serum creatinine overestimates glomerular filtration rate in cirrhosis. Plasma cystatin C may better reflect renal function and prognosis, but Indian data are scarce. We assessed cystatin C as a marker of ACLF and 28-day mortality in acutely decompensated cirrhosis. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 100 adults with acutely decompensated cirrhosis were enrolled over 18 months. We performed clinical assessments and standard investigations, and measured plasma cystatin C by nephelometric immunoassay within 48 hours of admission. Participants were followed for ACLF and 28-day mortality. Cystatin C, Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP), and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores were compared as predictors of mortality by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results: ACLF developed in 41 participants (41%), and 44 (44%) died within 28 days. Mean plasma cystatin C was higher in non-survivors than survivors (5.49±4.70 vs 2.06±1.54 mg/L; p<0.001) but did not differ by ACLF status (p=0.271). Cystatin C predicted 28-day mortality with AUROC 0.781 (95% CI 0.688-0.874); a cut-off ≥2.5 mg/L gave 73% sensitivity and 75% specificity, outperforming CTP (0.506) and MELD (0.508) scores (p<0.001). Conclusions: Plasma cystatin C rose in patients who died within 28 days and predicted short-term mortality better than CTP or MELD scores, although it did not discriminate ACLF status. Cystatin C may serve as a simple, reproducible adjunct for prognostication in decompensated cirrhosis; larger multicentric studies are needed to validate this cut-off. Introduction Cirrhosis typically evolves from a silent, compensated stage into a decompensated one, announced by ascites, variceal haemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy or jaundice. Most patients who decompensate acutely still have a reasonably favourable short-term outlook, with roughly 1.9% dying within 28 days; that figure climbs to almost 30% once acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) sets in [1]. Renal failure is the most common organ failure in ACLF and is associated with a worse prognosis than the failure of any other single organ [2]. Serum creatinine remains the most widely used marker of renal function because it is inexpensive and easily available, but its concentration is confounded by reduced muscle mass, low dietary protein intake and increased tubular secretion in cirrhosis, so that it systematically overestimates the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in this population [3,4]. Cystatin C, a low-molecular-weight cysteine-protease inhibitor produced by all nucleated cells at a constant rate and cleared almost exclusively by glomerular filtration, is a more sensitive marker of change in GFR than creatinine and correlates better with directly measured (inulin) clearance in patients with liver cirrhosis [5,6]. It rises within 12 to 24 hours of renal injury, earlier than creatinine, and is less influenced by muscle mass, diet, and bilirubin levels. In a large prospective European cohort, baseline plasma cystatin C independently predicted renal dysfunction, hepatorenal syndrome, ACLF and mortality in patients with acute decompensation of cirrhosis [7]. Data on plasma cystatin C in Indian patients with acutely decompensated cirrhosis are, however, scarce. The primary objective of this study was to assess plasma cystatin C as a predictor of 28-day mortality in patients with acute decompensation of cirrhosis, including its performance relative to the Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) scores. The secondary objective was to determine whether cystatin C level was associated with the development of ACLF. Note: Cystatin C was not evaluated and is not proposed here as a diagnostic test for ACLF itself. Materials & Methods This prospective, hospital-based observational cohort study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of General Medicine of a tertiary-care teaching hospital in New Delhi, India, along with the Department of Pathology. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College & Safdarjung Hospital (approval no. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Thesis/2019-10/55). Every participant gave written informed consent before enrolment. We screened consecutive adults (aged over 18 years) admitted for acute decompensation of cirrhosis, identified by new-onset or worsening ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, or gastrointestinal bleeding in someone with known cirrhosis, and excluded anyone with pre-existing renal disease or malignancy. All patients meeting these criteria during the enrolment period were included consecutively. None were excluded for missing data. A total of 100 participants completed the 28-day follow-up. The sample size was calculated from a prior report of cystatin C's diagnostic performance (73.3% sensitivity and 52.5% specificity for short-term mortality; 58.0% sensitivity and 66.4% specificity for ACLF) [7] at 80% power, a two-sided α of 0.05 and 15% allowable precision. This required at least 84 participants, so we enrolled 100 to build in a margin. Every participant had a detailed history and examination, abdominal ultrasonography, and venous blood drawn within 48 hours of admission for a complete blood count, renal and liver function tests, serum electrolytes, random blood glucose, viral markers (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV), and plasma cystatin C. Cystatin C was quantified by particle-enhanced immunonephelometry on a BN II System analyser (Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, DEU) using a 2 mL ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) sample per the manufacturer's assay protocol. Fasting was not required as cystatin C production and clearance are not materially affected by recent food intake. The GFR was estimated from the 2012 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation that combines creatinine and cystatin C [8]. We applied the Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL) consensus definition of ACLF, i.e., an acute hepatic insult presenting with jaundice (serum bilirubin above 5 mg/dL) and coagulopathy (international normalised ratio (INR) above 1.5), progressing to ascites and/or hepatic encephalopathy within four weeks in someone with chronic liver disease that may or may not have been recognised previously [9]. Consistent with the chronic liver failure-sequential organ failure assessment (CLIF-SOFA) renal subscore, a serum creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL was used to indicate renal dysfunction [1,10]. Severity of cirrhosis was graded using the CTP class and the MELD score. All participants were followed for the development of ACLF and for all-cause mortality up to 28 days from enrolment. We first checked continuous variables for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test; results are reported as numbers and percentages for categorical variables, and since most continuous measures departed from a normal distribution, we used the median (interquartile range) alongside the mean±SD for reference. Group comparisons accordingly relied on the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and on the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, with Fisher's test used whenever an expected cell count fell below five. To identify the plasma cystatin C threshold that best predicted 28-day mortality, we constructed a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and selected the cut-off that maximised the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity − 1); its area under the curve (AUC) was compared with that of the CTP and MELD scores, each computed in the same direction (death as the positive outcome), using DeLong's test. Significance was set at a two-sided p-value below 0.05, and all computations were carried out in SPSS Statistics version 21.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Results A total of 100 patients with acutely decompensated liver cirrhosis, recruited over 18 months, were included in the analysis. The mean (SD) age was 48.8 (10.1) years (median 48.5, range 29-76), with the largest proportion of participants (34%) in the 41-50-year age group; 82 (82%) were men. Alcohol was the commonest aetiology of cirrhosis (75 patients, 75%), followed by hepatitis B (10, 10%), hepatitis E (5, 5%) and hepatitis C (3, 3%); none of the participants was seropositive for HIV. On presentation, ascites was documented in 93 patients (93%), haematemesis/malena in 90 (90%), icterus in 89 (89%), hepatic encephalopathy in 88 (88%), pedal oedema in 64 (64%) and pallor in 61 (61%). Most participants were classified as CTP class C (79%), followed by class B (17%) and class A (4%); the median CTP score was 11 (IQR 10-12). The median MELD score was 34.3 (IQR 32.2-37.1), and 64% of participants had a MELD score of 30-39. Acute-on-chronic liver failure developed in 41 patients (41%), and 44 patients (44%) died within 28 days of enrolment. The overall mean (SD) plasma cystatin C was 3.57 (3.72) mg/L (median 2.16, IQR 1.13-4.03); 77 patients (77%) had a level above 1.11 mg/L. The association between clinical features and 28-day mortality is shown in Table 1. Icterus was significantly more frequent among non-survivors (p=0.021). Other clinical and aetiological features did not differ significantly between those who died and those who survived. Laboratory parameters associated with 28-day mortality were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, as none were normally distributed (Table 2). Platelet count, blood urea, serum creatinine, plasma cystatin C, and total, direct, and indirect bilirubin were all significantly higher among non-survivors (p<0.05 for all). Plasma cystatin C level did not differ significantly between patients with and without ACLF, either as a continuous variable (mean (SD) 4.31 (4.31) vs 3.05 (3.19) mg/L; p=0.271) or when dichotomised at 1.11 mg/L (83% vs 73% of patients above this cut-off; p=0.240); the strength of association was small (point-biserial r=0.17). In contrast, plasma cystatin C was strongly and significantly higher among patients who died within 28 days than among survivors (mean (SD) 5.49 (4.70) vs 2.06 (1.54) mg/L; median 3.70 vs 1.35 mg/L; Mann-Whitney U=1925, p<0.001), with a large effect size (point-biserial r=0.46). Among the 44 patients who died, 40 (91%) had a cystatin C level above 1.11 mg/L, compared with 37 of 56 survivors (66%; χ2=8.58, p=0.003). On ROC curve analysis, plasma cystatin C predicted 28-day mortality with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.781 (95% CI 0.688-0.874; p<0.001) (Figure 1). A cut-off of ≥2.5 mg/L gave a sensitivity of 73% (95% CI 57-85), specificity of 75% (95% CI 62-86), positive predictive value of 70% (95% CI 54-82), negative predictive value of 78% (95% CI 64-88) and diagnostic accuracy of 74% (95% CI 64-82); the odds ratio for 28-day mortality at this cut-off was 7.15 (95% CI 2.95-17.35). Diagnostic performance of cystatin C, CTP score, and MELD score for predicting 28-day mortality is compared in Table 3 and Figure 2. On DeLong's test, the AUROC for cystatin C was significantly higher than for the CTP score (0.506, 95% CI 0.392-0.620) or MELD score (0.508, 95% CI 0.392-0.624) (p<0.001 for both), while both the CTP and MELD scores did not differ significantly from each other (p=0.898). Discussion In this prospective cohort of 100 patients with acutely decompensated liver cirrhosis, plasma cystatin C was significantly elevated in patients who died within 28 days of admission and discriminated 28-day mortality substantially better than the conventional CTP and MELD scores, with a proposed cut-off of 2.5 mg/L yielding 73% sensitivity and 75% specificity. The cystatin C level, however, did not differ significantly between patients with and without ACLF, suggesting that in this cohort it performed better as a marker of short-term mortality risk than as a discriminator of ACLF itself. The prevalence of ACLF in our cohort (41%) is comparable to that reported in other prospective cohorts of acute decompensation of cirrhosis [7,11]. Our finding that plasma cystatin C rises significantly in patients who die within 28 days corroborates a large multicentre cohort in which baseline cystatin C independently predicted 90-day mortality, renal dysfunction, hepatorenal syndrome and ACLF [7], as well as reports from hepatitis B virus-related ACLF and decompensated cirrhosis in which a higher cystatin C level was associated with increased short-term mortality, and in which combining cystatin C with total bilirubin improved prediction of survival beyond conventional severity scores [11,12]. Cystatin C has similarly been reported to identify acute kidney injury earlier than creatinine and to independently predict outcome in other cohorts of cirrhosis, with proposed cut-offs in a range comparable to ours [13-15]. Unlike some of these reports, we did not find a significant association between cystatin C level and ACLF status itself; this may reflect differences in the criteria used to define ACLF, in disease severity, or in sample size across studies. The limited discrimination we observed for the CTP and MELD scores is in keeping with reports that conventional severity scores can perform inconsistently for short-term mortality prediction across ACLF cohorts and that other markers have sometimes outperformed them [16]. It may also reflect the referral bias of a tertiary-care centre, where nearly four-fifths of our participants were already in CTP class C, narrowing the range over which these scores could discriminate outcome. A few limitations temper these findings. The work was carried out at one tertiary-care centre with no liver-transplant programme, and none of our participants were transplanted during follow-up. This probably contributed to the relatively high mortality we observed and limits how far the results can be extended to centres where transplantation is available. As an observational study, it can establish association but not causation, and our cohort was predominantly male and alcohol-related with a high proportion of CTP class C disease, which may limit generalisability to milder or aetiologically different populations. The sample size, while adequate for the pre-specified diagnostic-accuracy calculations, limited subgroup analysis by aetiology or organ-failure pattern; we also relied on univariable comparisons and ROC analysis rather than multivariable regression, so we cannot exclude confounding by variables such as age or bilirubin, and the proposed cystatin C cut-off requires external, ideally multivariable, validation before clinical use. Strengths include the prospective design, pre-specified sample-size calculation, and head-to-head comparison of cystatin C with two established prognostic scores in the same cohort using the same outcome definition; this is consistent with reports that cystatin C-based measures can add incremental value for the early detection of renal impairment even in milder disease [17]. Conclusions In this cohort, plasma cystatin C measured within 48 hours of admission was associated with a greater risk of death during the subsequent 28 days and showed better mortality discrimination than the CTP or MELD scores. It did not, however, distinguish ACLF status. Confirmation in larger multicentre cohorts is needed before the proposed 2.5 mg/L threshold can be applied clinically. If validated, cystatin C may provide a practical adjunct to established prognostic assessment in acutely decompensated cirrhosis. records.content: Abstract Background: Chronic liver disease (CLD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with India accounting for the highest absolute number of cirrhosis-related deaths globally. Serum uric acid (SUA), the end product of purine metabolism, is increasingly recognised as a marker of oxidative stress and metabolic derangement and has been reported to be elevated in CLD. The Child-Pugh score remains the most widely used bedside tool for assessing hepatic functional reserve. Data regarding the association of SUA with Child-Pugh class and CLD-related complications in Indian tertiary care settings remain limited. Objectives: The study aimed to estimate SUA levels in patients with CLD at admission, determine their association with disease severity according to Child-Pugh class, and assess their association with CLD-related complications. Methods: This cross-sectional, observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of General Medicine at a tertiary care teaching hospital. Ninety-two consecutive patients with CLD aged 18-65 years were enrolled. Fasting SUA, liver function tests, haemogram, and coagulation parameters were recorded, and disease severity was graded using the Child-Pugh classification. Continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t-test or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons. Categorical associations were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. A two-tailed p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: The mean age was 47.6 years, with a male predominance (76.1%). Alcoholic liver disease was the most common aetiology (65.2%). Sixty-four (69.6%) patients had elevated SUA (>7.2 mg/dL, the cutoff applied uniformly to both sexes), with an overall mean SUA of 7.1 ± 1.9 mg/dL. Mean SUA increased progressively across Child-Pugh classes A (5.2 ± 1.1 mg/dL), B (6.9 ± 1.3 mg/dL), and C (8.4 ± 1.6 mg/dL) (ANOVA F(2,89)=37.38, p<0.001), with all pairwise comparisons significant after Bonferroni correction (all p<0.001). SUA was also significantly associated with Child-Pugh class in categorical analysis (χ2(2)=22.00, p<0.001). Patients with complications had higher mean SUA than those without complications (8.0 ± 1.5 vs. 5.6 ± 1.2 mg/dL; t(90)=8.08, p<0.001), and elevated SUA was significantly associated with any complication (χ2(1)=17.63, p<0.001). Child-Pugh class was similarly associated with complications (χ2(2)=15.68, p<0.001). Among individual complications, elevated SUA was significantly associated with hepatic encephalopathy (χ2(1)=6.15, p=0.013) but not with variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, or portal hypertension (all p>0.05). Conclusion: Hyperuricaemia was common in this CLD cohort and was significantly associated with Child-Pugh class and the overall presence of complications. These findings support a hypothesis-generating association between SUA and disease severity rather than an established prognostic or independent role. Except for hepatic encephalopathy, SUA was not significantly associated with individual complications. Larger prospective multicentric studies adjusting for renal function and other confounders are needed before SUA can be considered a clinical adjunct marker. Introduction Chronic liver disease (CLD) is a progressive pathological process characterised by ongoing hepatocellular destruction and regeneration, culminating in fibrosis and cirrhosis [1]. Liver cirrhosis and other CLDs were responsible for approximately 1.47 million deaths worldwide in 2019, and India recorded the highest absolute number of deaths and disability-adjusted life-years attributable to this disease group of any single country [1]. Within the Asia-Pacific region, alcohol-related liver disease and chronic viral hepatitis B and C remain the dominant aetiologies, with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) emerging as a rapidly growing contributor amid the region's changing dietary and metabolic profile [2]. Uric acid is the terminal product of purine catabolism, generated predominantly in the liver and intestine through the sequential oxidation of hypoxanthine and xanthine by xanthine oxidase. Beyond its traditional association with gout and nephrolithiasis, elevated serum uric acid (SUA) is now recognised as a marker of oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and low-grade systemic inflammation -- mechanisms that are also implicated in metabolic syndrome and progressive hepatic injury [3]. In the setting of CLD, hyperuricaemia has been attributed to a combination of increased purine turnover from hepatocyte necrosis, reduced hepatic and renal clearance of urate as synthetic and excretory function deteriorates, and the metabolic derangements that accompany portal hypertension and diuretic therapy. Population-based data from the United States have shown that an elevated SUA level is independently associated with both the development of cirrhosis and the presence of elevated hepatic transaminases, even after adjustment for established risk factors [4]. A similar mechanistic link between hyperuricaemia and progressive fatty liver disease -- via insulin resistance, hepatic lipogenesis, and inflammasome activation -- has been described in patients with NAFLD [5]. The Child-Pugh score (originally the Child-Turcotte classification [6], later modified by Pugh and colleagues to replace nutritional status with prothrombin time [7]) remains the most widely used bedside tool for grading the severity of hepatic dysfunction and for predicting short- and medium-term survival in patients with cirrhosis. It combines two laboratory variables (serum bilirubin and albumin) with three clinical or coagulation variables (prothrombin time/international normalised ratio (INR), ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy) to stratify patients into Class A, B, or C, corresponding to one-year survival rates of approximately 100%, 81%, and 45%, respectively. Although newer objective scores such as the model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) have gained prominence [8], particularly for transplant allocation, the Child-Pugh score continues to be favoured in routine clinical practice for its simplicity and bedside applicability [9]. Several small, single-centre studies from South Asia have reported a positive association between SUA level and Child-Pugh class, suggesting that SUA could serve as an inexpensive, widely available adjunct to existing severity-scoring systems [10,11]. However, the strength of this association, and its relationship with specific disease complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, has varied across studies and study populations, and dedicated Indian tertiary care data remain limited. Establishing this relationship more precisely could support the use of SUA as a low-cost tool for early risk stratification, particularly in resource-constrained settings where its estimation is already inexpensive and widely accessible. The present study was therefore undertaken to estimate SUA levels at admission in patients with CLD attending a tertiary care teaching hospital, to determine the association between SUA level and disease severity as graded by the Child-Pugh score, and, as a secondary objective, to study the association between SUA level and CLD-related complications. Materials & Methods Study design and setting This was a hospital-based, cross-sectional, observational study conducted in the Department of General Medicine at NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Center and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India, from May 1, 2024, to October 31, 2025. Patients with a diagnosis of CLD were screened consecutively over a period of 18 consecutive months, as they presented to the department. The study was conducted after obtaining approval from the institutional ethics committee (IEC Reference No. 29/2024; approval date: April 18, 2024), and it was carried out in accordance with the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before enrolment. Sample size calculation As no comparable prior study had reported an effect size for the primary association between SUA and Child-Pugh class that could be used for a formal a priori power calculation, the sample size was instead estimated using the anticipated proportion of raised SUA among patients with CLD reported in a prior study from a comparable tertiary care setting (anticipated proportion = 40%) [10], as a pragmatic basis for ensuring an adequately sized cohort. Using the standard formula for estimating a single proportion with a fixed absolute precision, where Z1−a is the standard normal deviate corresponding to a two-tailed alpha error of 5% (1.96), p is the anticipated proportion (0.40), and d is the absolute precision (±10%), the calculated minimum sample size was 92. All 92 subjects fulfilling the eligibility criteria during the study period were enrolled by consecutive sampling. This proportion-based justification, rather than a formal power calculation for the primary SUA-Child-Pugh class association, is acknowledged as a limitation of the study design (see Limitations). Participants Patients were enrolled consecutively, as they presented and met the following eligibility criteria. Patients aged 18-65 years of either sex with a clinical, biochemical, and/or imaging-based diagnosis of CLD, who were willing to participate, were included. Patients with a history of malignancy (leukaemia or lymphoma), gout, chronic kidney disease (defined as a pre-existing clinical diagnosis of chronic kidney disease or a documented estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for >3 months, based on history and available prior records), those on drugs known to affect serum urate (frusemide, thiazide diuretics, allopurinol, or febuxostat), those undergoing chemotherapy, those with recent major surgery or trauma, and those who did not provide informed consent were excluded. Acute kidney injury at presentation was not used as a separate exclusion criterion, other than where it manifested as hepatorenal syndrome, which was captured as a study complication; serial serum creatinine measurements were not systematically available for all participants to permit a formal, protocol-driven assessment of acute kidney injury by standard consensus criteria, and this is discussed further as a limitation. Data collection A detailed history (including age, sex, socio-economic status, and relevant lifestyle factors such as alcohol use) and a thorough clinical examination, including a systemic examination directed at features of CLD, were performed and recorded on a structured case record form for every participant. Relevant risk factors and comorbidities elicited on history and examination were also recorded. Procedure Venous blood samples were drawn after an overnight fast at the time of admission, before the initiation of any drug that could alter SUA level. Complete blood count was estimated on an automated five-part haematology analyser (Siemens Advia 2120). Fasting and post-prandial blood glucose were measured by the glucose oxidase-peroxidase method. Lipid profile was assessed on a Siemens Dimension RxL Max analyser, with total cholesterol measured by the cholesterol oxidase-peroxidase method, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol by a direct (polyethene glycol-modified enzyme) method, and triglycerides by an enzymatic endpoint method. SUA was estimated by the uricase-peroxidase (enzymatic colorimetric) method on the same Siemens Dimension RxL Max autoanalyser. A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram was recorded using a Schiller AT-2 plus machine where clinically indicated. Liver function tests (serum bilirubin, direct and indirect fractions, aspartate and alanine aminotransferases, and serum albumin) and prothrombin time/INR were estimated by standard laboratory methods on the day of admission. Disease severity was graded using the Child-Turcotte-Pugh classification, which assigns 1-3 points each for serum bilirubin, serum albumin, prothrombin time prolongation (or INR), ascites, and grade of hepatic encephalopathy; the summed score classifies patients as Class A (5-6 points), Class B (7-9 points), or Class C (10-15 points) [7]. Presence of complications was recorded on the basis of standard clinical, biochemical, endoscopic, and/or imaging criteria at the time of the index admission, applying published consensus definitions: hepatic encephalopathy was graded clinically using the West Haven criteria [12]; variceal bleed and clinically evident portal hypertension were defined by endoscopic and/or imaging evidence of oesophagogastric varices with or without active or recent bleeding [13]; hepatorenal syndrome was defined using the revised International Club of Ascites-acute kidney injury (ICA-AKI) criteria [14]; and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis was defined as an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count >250 cells/mm3 in the absence of a secondary source of infection [15]. Data were entered into a password-protected electronic spreadsheet, verified weekly for accuracy, and kept confidential throughout the study. Outcome measures The primary outcome measures were (i) the SUA level at admission, categorised as normal (≤ 7.2 mg/dL) or elevated (> 7.2 mg/dL), and its association with Child-Pugh class (A, B, or C); and (ii) the mean SUA level compared across Child-Pugh classes and between patients with and without complications. A single cutoff of 7.2 mg/dL, corresponding to the upper limit of the standard laboratory reference range in males, was applied uniformly to both sexes for categorisation, consistent with the approach used in the comparable prior studies referenced for sample size estimation and comparison [10,11]; because the standard upper reference limit is lower in females (approximately 6.0 mg/dL), this uniform threshold may under-detect hyperuricaemia in female participants, and this is discussed further as a limitation. The secondary outcome measure was the association between SUA level and the individual complications of CLD (hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and portal hypertension). Statistical analysis Data were entered into Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington) and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 20 (released 2011; IBM Corp., Armonk, New York). Descriptive statistics are presented as mean ± standard deviation for continuous variables and as frequency (percentage) for categorical variables. For continuous outcomes, the independent-samples Student's t-test was used to compare SUA levels between two groups (presence vs. absence of complications), and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the F-test was used to compare SUA levels across the three Child-Pugh classes; where the omnibus F-test was significant, pairwise comparisons between each pair of classes (A vs. B, A vs. C, B vs. C) were performed using pooled-variance t-tests with Bonferroni correction for three comparisons. For each categorical association, a single primary test was selected a priori based on table dimensions and expected cell counts: the Pearson chi-square test of independence (uncorrected) was used for all contingency tables in which no more than 20% of cells had an expected count of <5. Fisher's exact test was used instead wherever this assumption was violated, as recommended for sparse tables [16]. A two-tailed p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant throughout. Ethical declaration The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and all participants provided written informed consent after being explained the purpose, procedures, and potential risks and benefits of participation. Participants were informed of their right to withdraw at any stage without any effect on their clinical care, and confidentiality of all data was maintained throughout the study. Results A total of 92 patients with CLD fulfilling the eligibility criteria were enrolled consecutively over the 18-month study period. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarised in Table 1. The majority of participants were middle-aged, with the highest proportion in the 51-60-year age group (30.4%) and the lowest below 30 years of age (8.7%); the mean age of the cohort was 47.6 years (calculated from grouped data). There was a marked male predominance (76.1%). Alcoholic liver disease was the leading aetiology (65.2%), followed by NAFLD (15.2%), viral hepatitis (10.9%), and cryptogenic cirrhosis (8.7%). On admission, 64 of 92 (69.6%) patients had an elevated SUA level (>7.2 mg/dL), and 70 of 92 (76.1%) patients were classified as Child-Pugh Class B or C, reflecting a cohort weighted towards moderate-to-advanced hepatic dysfunction at presentation. Distribution of complications among study participants has been presented in Table 2. Hepatic encephalopathy was the most frequent complication (32.6%), followed by portal hypertension (28.3%), variceal bleeding (21.7%), hepatorenal syndrome (13.0%), and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (8.7%). Laboratory parameters of study participants has been presented in Table 3. Mean haemoglobin was 10.8 ± 1.9 g/dL, consistent with mild anaemia, and the mean platelet count was at the lower end of the normal range (1.85 ± 0.72 × 105/mm3). Transaminases and bilirubin were elevated, and serum albumin was reduced, in keeping with impaired synthetic and excretory hepatic function. The overall mean SUA level was 7.1 ± 1.9 mg/dL. This retrospective analysis evaluated data from the Precision-T phase 1b multicenter study comparing TREGZI + tacrolimus (Tac) to a CIBMTR-NMDP registry cohort of patients receiving conventional allo-HSCT + PTCy based GVHD prophylaxis. The findings, featured in the journal Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, showed improved survival outcomes for patients treated with TREGZI compared to similar patients treated with PTCy in the myeloablative setting. The data published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy reinforce the potential role of high-precision graft engineering platforms and therapeutic interventions like TREGZI, in improving long-term outcomes in patients with blood cancer. “Allogeneic stem cell transplant has long been considered the only curative option for advanced hematologic malignancies, but the risks associated with them – including graft versus host disease (GVHD) – are potentially life threatening,” said Caspian Oliai, MD, medical director of the UCLA Bone Marrow Transplantation Stem Cell Processing Center. “While there are treatment options available to help prevent GVHD, data on the impact of them on overall survival have been limited. The findings from this retrospective analysis on the recently approved therapy, TREGZI, point to the value of cell therapy in potentially improving transplant outcomes for patients without sacrificing long-term survival.” The TREGZI arm was associated with higher OS over a three-year follow-up period compared to PTCy arm (HR=0.41; log-rank p=0.003). Overall survival at one, two, and three years for patients receiving TREGZI (n=76) was 96% (95% CI: 88%-99%), 86% (76%-92%), and 83% (73%-90%), respectively. For patients included in the PTCy cohort (n=360), OS at one, two, and three years was 81% (95% CI:77%-85%), 72% (67%-77%), and 66% (60%-71%), respectively. Historically, a drug cocktail of Tacrolimus/methotrexate (tac/MTX) was the predominant standard of care to prevent GVHD for patients following alloHSCT. However, there has been increased adoption of different approaches to GVHD prevention such as, PTCy-based regimens and the recently approved high-precision cell therapy, TREGZI. In clinical studies, both TREGZI + Tac and allo-HSCT + PTCy have demonstrated the reduced cumulative incidence of GVHD relative to Tac/MTX. “We welcome the publication of these data in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy as it contributes to the body of evidence that supports the therapeutic value of graft engineering approaches in GVHD,” said Nate Fernhoff, co-founder and CEO, Orca Bio. “We are a company committed to redefining what’s possible for patients in allogeneic cell therapy, and these data reinforce the value of Orca Bio’s technology in the durable restoration of a healthy immune system and reducing treatment-related toxicities in patients with blood cancer.” About the Phase 1b Study and Comparative Analysis The data published in Transplantation and Cellular Therapy, were based on a retrospective analysis of long-term survival follow up from a Phase 1b multicenter trial evaluating TREGZI for the treatment of hematologic malignancies, data from which have been presented at multiple scientific congresses including the American Society of Hematology (ASH) and the Tandem meetings of ASTCTTM and CIBMTRTM. The three-year OS outcomes observed with TREGZI were compared to a historical cohort of patients receiving an allogeneic stem cell transplant with PTCy-based GVHD prophylaxis. The cohort included was from registry data collected by CIBMTR-NMDP. The inclusion criteria for this comparative analysis were similar to those of the TREGZI Precision-T Phase 3 trial including: patients who were ≤65 years of age with confirmed diagnoses of either intermediate- or high-risk acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in complete remission or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), who were treated with a myeloablative conditioning (MAC) regimen, and an 8/8 HLA-matched donor. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION AND INDICATION WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Graft Failure: Graft failure has occurred after TREGZI administration. Screen TREGZI recipients for antidonor antibodies that may prevent engraftment. Monitor patients closely for laboratory evidence of hematopoietic recovery. Graft-Versus-Host Disease: Acute and chronic Graft-Versus-Host disease (GVHD), including life-threatening and fatal cases, occurred following treatment with TREGZI. Acute GVHD manifests as maculopapular rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, and elevated bilirubin. Chronic GVHD may include skin rash, mouth sores, dry eyes, liver inflammation, and development of scar tissue in the skin and joints and damage to the lungs. Treat patients with a single agent calcineurin inhibitor as prophylaxis to decrease the risk of GVHD. Monitor for signs and symptoms of GVHD, and treat if GVHD develops. Infusion Reactions: Infusion reactions (IRs) may occur during or following treatment with TREGZI. Serious hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis may occur to DMSO, human serum albumin (HSA), Dextran or murine protein present in TREGZI. IRs may begin within minutes of the start of TREGZI infusion, although symptoms may continue to intensify and not peak for several hours after the completion of the infusion. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of IRs during and after TREGZI administration. When a reaction occurs, pause the infusion and institute supportive care as needed. Premedicate patients with antipyretics and histamine antagonists prior to infusion to reduce the incidence and intensity of infusion reactions. Secondary Malignancies and Malignancies of Donor Origin: Secondary malignancies and malignancies of donor origin may occur following treatment with TREGZI. Development of secondary malignancies, including posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) may occur many years after transplantation. PTLD manifests as a lymphoma-like disease favoring non-nodal sites. PTLD is usually fatal if not treated. Serial monitoring of blood for EBV DNA may be warranted in patients with persistent cytopenias. No patient treated with TREGZI has developed PTLD. Monitor for malignancies of donor origin and secondary malignancies. Contact Orca Bio at 1-877-411-6722 if any patient is diagnosed with a secondary malignancy or a malignancy of donor origin. Transmission of Infectious Agents: Transmission of serious infectious or communicable disease or agents may occur with TREGZI treatment as it is derived from human donor blood and manufactured using animal-derived reagents. Risks of transmission of infectious agents may occur despite screening or testing of donors. Risks of transmission of serious infections include, but are not limited to, human immunodeficiency virus, human T cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV)-1 and -2, hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Treponema pallidum, Trypanosoma cruzi, West Nile virus (WNV), cytomegalovirus, transmissible spongiform encephalopathy agents and vaccinia. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of infections, perform tests for infectious agents and treat as clinically indicated. ADVERSE REACTIONS The most common adverse reactions (incidence ≥ 20%) were mucositis, diarrhea, rash, viral infections, infections pathogen unspecified, abdominal pain, vomiting, nausea, bacterial infections, hemorrhage, aGVHD, edema, and fungal infections. It is indicated for use in matched donor hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with myeloablative preparative regimen, for hematopoietic and immunologic reconstitution and to improve chronic graft-versus-host-disease-free survival, in the treatment of adults with hematological malignancies. TREGZI is a personalized treatment manufactured for each individual patient using living cells from a matched donor. TREGZI uses hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) to reconstitute the immune system, highly purified regulatory T cells (Tregs) to suppress GVHD and conventional T cells (Tcons) to accelerate immune reconstitution and produce graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) activity. The FDA approval of TREGZI was based on the results of Precision-T, a randomized, open-label, multi-center study that evaluated the safety, efficacy and tolerability of TREGZI compared with conventional allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (alloHSCT). With the testing completed and the WCB now successfully established, Avaí Bio and Austrianova have completed an important milestone in the development of the Company’s genetically modified α-Klotho-producing cell line. The testing confirmed that the MCB, and in turn, the WCB are free of a broad range of potentially contaminating viruses and other adventitious agents. The testing included more than 30 viruses, including significant human and animal pathogens such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), and hepatitis B and C viruses.
